name: Ahaz (son of Jotham)
title: Ahaz – The Apostate and Idolatrous King of Judah
summary: Ahaz marked a deep spiritual collapse in the royal line of the kingdom of Judah. Despite his father Jotham’s godly legacy, he introduced Canaanite idolatry on a large scale and even went so far as to sacrifice his own children by fire in the Valley of Hinnom. During the Syro-Ephraimite war, when Syria and the northern kingdom of Israel threatened Jerusalem, he rejected the prophet Isaiah’s call to trust in God. Instead, he chose to submit as a vassal to the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III, paying tribute with treasures from both the temple and the royal treasury. He also had a pagan altar built according to an Assyrian-Syrian pattern in the Lord’s temple and reorganized its worship. During his sixteen years of reign, Judah suffered repeated military defeats from several directions—Syria, Israel, Edom, and the Philistines—which were interpreted as God’s judgment on the king’s apostasy. The condemnation of Ahaz was so severe that, according to Chronicles, he was denied a place in the royal tombs after his death.

keyEvents.title: Becomes King of Judah
keyEvents.description: Ahaz became king at the age of twenty and reigned for sixteen years in Jerusalem. He did not walk in the ways of the Lord as his ancestor David, but followed the ways of the kings of Israel.

keyEvents.title: Sacrifices His Children to Idols
keyEvents.description: Ahaz made his son pass through the fire according to the detestable practices of the nations whom the Lord had driven out before the people of Israel. He sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on the hills and under every green tree.

keyEvents.title: The Syro-Ephraimite War and the Immanuel Sign
keyEvents.description: King Rezin of Syria and King Pekah of Israel threatened Jerusalem. The prophet Isaiah met Ahaz with a promise that the enemies' plans would not succeed, and urged him to ask for a sign from the Lord. When Ahaz refused, Isaiah gave the famous Immanuel sign.

keyEvents.title: Seeking Help from Assyria
keyEvents.description: Instead of trusting in God, Ahaz sent gold and silver from the temple and the royal treasury to the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III and submitted as a vassal to gain military help against Syria and Israel.

keyEvents.title: Building a Pagan Altar in the Temple
keyEvents.description: After seeing an altar in Damascus during a meeting with the Assyrian king, Ahaz had priest Uriah build a copy and set it up in the Lord's temple. He changed the temple worship and removed several of the temple's holy objects.

keyEvents.title: Ahaz's Death and Dishonorable Burial
keyEvents.description: Ahaz died and was buried in Jerusalem, but according to Chronicles he was not laid among the graves of the kings of Judah—a clear sign of condemnation for his reign. His son Hezekiah became king after him.

versions.summary: Ahaz was king of Judah and son of the godly Jotham. He was one of the most wicked kings in Judah's history, introducing idolatry and even sacrificing his own son to the idol Molech. His reign was marked by foreign policy crisis and spiritual decline.
versions.title: The Wicked King of Judah
versions.reason: [major] Ahaz's lifespan is given as approx. 735-715 BC, but this does not match the chronology. He became king at age 20 and reigned for 16 years. His reign is usually dated to approx. 735-715 BC, but then he would have been born around 755 BC and died around 715 BC. The lifespan should reflect birth to death, not just the period of reign.; [major] Abi (or Abijah) was not Ahaz's wife, but Hezekiah's mother. According to 2 Kgs 18:2, 'Abi daughter of Zechariah' was Hezekiah's mother. This means that Abi was actually Ahaz's wife/one of his wives. But the ID 'abi' should be verified. In 2 Chr 29:1 she is called Abijah. The name is correctly linked as Hezekiah's mother and thus Ahaz's wife, but it is common to use the form 'abijah' as an ID.; [minor] The roles could be expanded to include that Ahaz was an idolater/apostate king, which is central to his character in biblical portrayal.; [minor] The summary is good, but could advantageously mention his meeting with the prophet Isaiah and the Immanuel sign (Isa 7:14), which is one of the most well-known events connected to Ahaz.; [minor] The description of the Syro-Ephraimite war could note that Ahaz refused to ask for a sign from the Lord, and that Isaiah then gave the Immanuel sign (Isa 7:10-14). The verse selection is good but skips verses 5-9 which provide important context.; [minor] The description says that Ahaz was not buried in the royal tombs, which agrees with 2 Chr 28:27. But it also states that Hezekiah 'reversed his father's ungodly reforms' – this is correct but the reference points only to the burial verse. Hezekiah's reforms are described elsewhere (2 Kgs 18; 2 Chr 29-31).; [major] Footnotes are missing. Ahaz is an important figure with rich historical, archaeological and theological connections that should be documented.

versions.summary: Ahaz was king of Judah and the son of the godly Jotham. He was one of the most wicked kings in Judah's history, who introduced idolatry and even had his son pass through the fire as an offering to Molech. During the Syro-Ephraimite war, he refused to trust in God and rejected the prophet Isaiah's call to ask for a sign from the Lord, who then gave the famous Immanuel sign. Instead, Ahaz sought help from the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser, built a pagan altar in the temple, and undermined worship in Jerusalem. His reign was marked by foreign policy crisis and deep spiritual decay.

versions.summary: As the son of the godly Jotham, Ahaz represented a dramatic turning point in the history of the kingdom of Judah. He introduced Canaanite idolatry on a large scale, including the abhorrent practice of child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom. When Syria and the northern kingdom of Israel threatened Jerusalem during the Syro-Ephraimite War, Ahaz refused to listen to the prophet Isaiah or place his trust in God. Instead, he submitted as a vassal to the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III and paid tribute using treasures from the temple and the royal treasury. He also built a pagan altar modeled after Assyrian-Syrian designs in the Lord's temple and reorganized the worship service. Ahaz's sixteen-year reign was marked by military defeats, foreign policy dependence, and deep spiritual decay. The condemnation of his rule was so severe that according to Chronicles he was not buried in the royal tombs.

footnotes.text: The name Ahaz (Hebrew: אָחָז, ʾĀḥāz) means 'he has seized' or 'he holds fast'. It is likely a shortened form of Jehoahaz ('the Lord has seized'). In Assyrian source texts the full form 'Ia-ú-ḫa-zi' (Jehoahaz of Judah) is used, confirming that the shorter biblical form is an abbreviation. A seal ring with the inscription 'belonging to Ahaz, (son of) Jotham' has been found, but its authenticity is debated among scholars.

The Syro-Ephraimite War (c. 735–732 BC) is well documented in Assyrian sources. Tiglath-Pileser III's annals confirm the conquest of Damascus and the deposition of King Rezin, as well as Ahaz's tribute to Assyria. The tribute text mentions gold, silver, and other valuables, consistent with the biblical account in 2 Kings 16:8.

The Immanuel prophecy in Isaiah 7:14, given in the context of Ahaz's unbelief, has a rich interpretive history. In its original historical setting, the sign served as a promise that the threat from Syria and Israel would soon disappear. In Christian tradition, the prophecy was interpreted as a messianic prophecy about Jesus' virgin birth (cf. Matt 1:23). The Hebrew term 'almah' (young woman) was translated with 'parthenos' (virgin) in the Septuagint, which has been central to the theological debate over the scope of the prophecy.

The expression to make one's son 'pass through the fire' (2 Kings 16:3) is linked to the Molech cult that was widespread among Canaanite and Phoenician peoples. Archaeological finds from Tophet sanctuaries in Carthage and other Phoenician colonies confirm the practice of child sacrifice in the Phoenician-Punic cultural sphere. The practice was strictly forbidden in the Law of Moses (Lev 18:21; Deut 18:10).

The Valley of Hinnom (Hebrew: Ge-Hinnom) south of Jerusalem, where Ahaz performed child sacrifices, later became strongly associated with idolatry and God's judgment. In New Testament times the Greek 'Gehenna' (derived from Ge-Hinnom) was used as a term for the place of destruction, showing the lasting theological impact of the site's history.

According to 2 Chronicles 28, Judah suffered major military defeats during Ahaz's reign—Syria took captives to Damascus, the northern kingdom of Israel inflicted a catastrophic defeat, and Edomites and Philistines attacked from other directions. The books of Chronicles consistently interpret these defeats as God's judgment on Ahaz's apostasy, in line with Deuteronomistic theology that disobedience to God leads to national disasters.

Ahaz's burial outside the royal tombs (2 Chron 28:27) was a strong symbolic condemnation. In the ancient Near East, burial location was an important expression of honor. The Chronicler's specific mention of this detail underscores the theological point that Ahaz's apostasy had lasting consequences for his legacy.
